part_title: Amazon Q Developer for AWS and Coding Workflows
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 7 through 10 individually in source order, verifying visible labels, workflows, examples, access-control boundaries, and service distinctions; rewritten as balanced-length teaching narration.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer
scenes.narration: Amazon Q Developer is an AI assistant for software development and AWS tasks. Begin with the left-hand requests: 'List my Lambda functions in this account' and 'Which AWS service should I use?' The middle panels show the assistant drawing on AWS documentation, service guidance and permitted AWS account context where supported. Its responses can include suggested AWS CLI commands, architecture ideas and troubleshooting steps. In the bottom-left example, Q Developer suggests the command aws lambda list-functions with a chosen Region. The developer runs it in an authorized environment to obtain the actual inventory; the command alone is not proof that functions exist. The second example asks about a low-administration serverless API. The pictured suggestion combines AWS Lambda for running code without managing servers and Amazon API Gateway for presenting an HTTP API. Notice the action-permissions panel on the right. Suggested commands and code still require review, credentials and authorized execution. Finally compare Q Developer with Q Business at the bottom. Developer focuses on AWS operations and coding, while Business retrieves answers from company knowledge. Do not confuse a helpful recommendation with permission to make changes.

scenes.title: AWS operations and costs
scenes.narration: This slide shows two operational uses of Amazon Q Developer. On the left, billing data flows from AWS Billing and Cost Management or Cost Explorer into a cost-analysis question. The illustrated user asks why AWS costs increased last month and requests the top drivers. Q Developer can help explain which services, accounts or usage patterns account for the change and suggest where to investigate optimization. It cannot invent a trustworthy cost total without relevant access and real data. On the right, a Lambda function produces an error, with CloudWatch holding the relevant logs and metrics. Read the example log: 'Task timed out after 3.00 seconds.' The assistant uses that symptom to suggest checking the timeout configuration, dependencies and permissions. But the log alone does not identify a single root cause. The lower decision strip asks which problem you have. For billing growth, inspect cost and usage records. For runtime failures, inspect CloudWatch logs and resource configuration. An assistant explains and proposes next steps; engineers verify the evidence and make controlled changes.

scenes.title: AI code companion
scenes.narration: This diagram shows Q Developer acting as a code companion inside an integrated development environment, or IDE, such as VS Code. Begin with the developer writing a natural-language request. The example asks for a Python boto3 function to list object keys in an S3 bucket. Boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python, and listing objects requires the proper S3 permissions. In the next panel, Q Developer suggests code or explains existing code using the relevant editor context. The third panel is intentionally human: the developer must review suggestions, edit them, run unit tests and check organizational security standards. Only then does the final panel commit approved code to source control and continue the normal deployment process. The checklist below reinforces that generated code is not automatically production-ready. Consider pagination, error handling and least-privilege credentials in the S3 example. The comparison on the right distinguishes code help from Amazon Q Business, which answers questions over company documents. The learning point is that AI can accelerate writing and understanding code, but correctness, security and the final commit remain the developer's responsibility.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer in IDE
scenes.narration: This slide is a code-security walkthrough in an IDE. Follow the upper sequence: a developer writes code, Q Developer suggests improvements, the developer tests the changes, and a security review identifies a possible issue. The lower worked example makes that issue concrete. The left code box assigns a literal API token, 'secret123', directly in source. Hard-coding credentials risks exposing them through repositories, logs or shared files. The suggested correction on the right retrieves the token at runtime using AWS Secrets Manager instead of embedding the secret in the script. The developer then edits and reviews the code, re-runs tests and confirms the security finding is resolved. Secrets Manager provides controlled secret storage and access; its permissions must still be configured securely. This is an illustrative snippet, not a complete production implementation. Read the bottom note as well: the slide flags an April 2027 support deadline for the legacy Q Developer IDE plugins, so check current AWS migration guidance before starting a new installation. Most importantly, an AI security suggestion is not an automatic repair. A human verifies code behavior and checks that real secrets were not already exposed.
